Lessons.Title: Quadratic Equations with Irrational Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: express irrational solutions of quadratic equations exactly using square roots, estimate their locations on a number line and distinguish exact expressions from decimal approximations. Independent first-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 15 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/15/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/15/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source reinforces that not every square-root solution simplifies to a rational number.

Original equation x²=7 has two real solutions ±√7. Because7 is not a perfect square integer, √7 is irrational, approximately2.64575; −√7≈−2.64575. The exact solution set is {−√7,√7}; rounding to2.65 would not satisfy the original equality exactly.

Second equation (x−4)²=3 yields x=4±√3. Both are irrational since adding rational4 to irrational √3 cannot make rational. Approximate values2.268 and5.732; the exact form exposes symmetry about x4. In contrast (x−4)²=9 gives rational roots1 and7.

Student task: solve both exact irrational examples and a rational contrast, plot approximations at sensible scale, and explain why an exact irrational root must not be called nonexistent merely because it is not a terminating decimal. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for complete ± solutions, exact forms, numerical approximations and justifications of irrationality.

KeyConcepts.Title: Irrational square root
KeyConcepts.Definition: The square root of a positive integer that is not a perfect square is irrational.
KeyConcepts.Rule: √7 cannot be represented as p/q for integers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Approximation versus equality
KeyConcepts.Definition: Decimal rounding provides a numerical location, not an exact equation identity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use exact radical for verified algebra.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Real irrational numbers are valid solutions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting only principal positive square root
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Square equations may have both signs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating approximate decimal with exact radical

SummaryPoints: Irrational roots can be written exactly using radicals.
x²=7 has roots ±√7; shifted square yields 4±√3.
Decimal approximations aid graphing but do not replace exact algebra.
Teacher reviews explanations and number-line placement.
